thread.title: Apple: 3 Things Tim Cook Didn't Tell You - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Stefan Redlich
title: Apple: 3 Things Tim Cook Didn't Tell You - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) made headlines early in the year when it unexpectedly and substantially cut its Q1 guidance to around $84B in sales compared to its earlier guidance range of $89B to $93B.
Source: apple.com
This was the first time since the launch of the iPhone in 2007 that Apple had to cut guidance and while a comprehensive " Letter from Tim Cook to Apple Investors " discussed several aspects, what is really important now for investors has not been raised.
Tim Cook cited an underestimated " magnitude of the economic deceleration, particularly in Greater China, " weaker-than-expected iPhone upgrades and the strength of the US dollar.
However, while all of these factors certainly played a role, this letter was not the "in-your-face-we-put-everything-out-now" type of honest investor information that one should have expected, particularly given how bullish Tim Cook still was during the November call.
Thus, I deep-dived into the letter and extracted the three key messages investors should really pay attention to. Unfortunately, as I see it, the whole environment for Apple is much more challenging than what the letter suggests and certainly a far cry away from Cook's bullish euphoria earlier in 2018 when he labeled the business "the best market in the world."
1) It's not the best market in the world During the earnings call of the June quarter last year, Tim Cook bullishly termed the market in which Apple is operating in to be " the best market for a consumer product company in the history of the world " to be in. Well, that was certainly true in the past but now that iPhone's exorbitant prices have hit a wall and competitors are also firing on all cylinders the picture has changed.
In fact, the overall smartphone market is expected to have declined by around 3% in 2018. It shows that although some younger smartphone makers, like Huawei and Xiaomi, have seen staggering growth in the market, the major players have difficulties in sustaining growth. Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) has been facing these problems with its Galaxy flagship series for a long time, but Apple was able to post strong growth as it could charge higher prices and significantly lift its top-line despite not selling any more units.
It looked as if Apple was immune to deteriorating industry dynamics and that was certainly true as long as two factors were valid:
1) The ability to charge higher prices for every new model bringing up ASP.
2) The market was not saturated in terms of customers that want to buy their first smartphone.
Now, after a decade of iPhone and other smartphones, virtually everybody who needs one got one and many have been using the same model for years. This means it is not about bringing customers to buy their first smartphone but rather getting them to upgrade their current smartphone. This situation was substantially aggravated by the fact that Apple's " Throttlegate " has forced the company to replace batteries for older models at firesale prices. Customers with 2-, 3- and 4-year old models were able to replace their dying battery with a new one for not even $50. These customers have no real incentive to upgrade to a new iPhone which is at least double but potentially even triple the price of their old one.
Apple is not immune to these dynamics and while that letter from Cook was a wake-up call, it came far too late. Apple mentioned during the last call it won't disclose units any more while at the same time saying everything is well and that especially in China the company does not see any slowdown. The writing was on the wall but Apple was dishonest or at least too proud to admit it had failed.
It now needs to come up with enticing features for future iPhones in order to attract these upgrade customers. The company can no longer afford to sell ultra-expensive hardware that only marginally differs from its predecessor. It also needs to competitively fight with Huawei and Xiaomi and not let them distribute the market for affordable low-end smartphones among themselves.
Huawei is now already the world's second-largest smartphone manufacturer and innovative rivals like Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo are rapidly catching up to Apple. While Apple still enjoys the luxury of dominating the ultra-premium smartphone market, things can quickly change especially if Apple continues to release these slightly-altered versions. Also, while margins in Apple's market segment are still sky-high, the writing is on the wall that this segment will become a smaller portion of the market unless some break-through features are released that will be exclusive to this price tier.
2) Apple needs to preserve its brand Anecdotal evidence (reading comments on the SA platform, reading articles and talking to people) has it that in the past Apple was mostly associated with "cool" and "wow" but following the Throttlegate, associations like "dishonest," "expensive" and "greedy" come into play. While that is not a scientific and representative evaluation I can certainly relate to these things, at least in terms that this is a risk. Apple is still the most valuable brand in the world and customers are willing to pay a premium for its products but even the strongest brand can sacrifice itself if it gets too expensive and elite. The latest iPhone generation has been a flop as its main features like face recognition, better camera and faster CPU are just not enough to pay the premium prices.
Apple's competitors have happily embraced that development, launching and establishing their own high-end but more affordable smartphone series, most notably Huawei's P-series and Mate-series. Apple still enjoys the enormous benefit of its tightly-integrated ecosystem which makes customers very loyal to the platform but it certainly should not stretch things too far.
3) iPhones falling off a cliff, down 15% Y/Y The revised guidance is 7.6% lower from the mid-point of the previous guidance which at first does not look too bad. Also, it is roughly 5% lower Y/Y.
In his letter Tim Cook mentioned that " In fact, categories outside of iPhone (Services, Mac, iPad, Wearables/Home/Accessories) combined to grow almost 19 percent year-over-year. "
With this statement Tim Cook revealed something which I am not sure he wanted to. In Q1/2018, Apple reported non-iPhone revenues of $26.7B which have now increased 19% to $31.8B. Apple's iPhone revenues for Q1/2018 came in at $61.6B and thus in order to arrive at around $84B for Q1/2019 iPhone revenue would have to come in at $52.2B. That is 15% down Y/Y and looks much more serious than the overall 5% Y/Y decline.
If management was really that clueless about such a sizable drop despite already factoring in various risks in its guidance, this very likely suggests that it has completely underestimated the impact of charging astronomical prices on its iPhones. That could have also been the real reason why Apple suddenly decided to no longer disclose unit sales. Disclosing those now or latest during the actual earnings release would allow us to understand whether the slowdown is driven despite higher ASPs or following lower ASPs. Higher ASPs would actually be a positive thing as it would imply that it can still charge premium prices but desperately also needs some products for the lower end segment. Given that Apple's guidance on gross margins remains unchanged, it looks to the former but there is nowhere to know and I expect virtually every analyst to dig into this during the call. Ultimately, despite Apple famously pronouncing units are no longer as important to the company as in the past, this quarter could have changed everything and the company will be forced to disclose units again.
Also, as Elazar succinctly pointed out in his piece, there is substantial revenue risk for the next quarters as well. For Q2, he estimates a big drop down to $55B in revenues, down around 10% Y/Y and a far cry from analysts' estimates which are still calling for around $60B . That guidance risk is something investors should be aware of even though positive developments on trade negotiations could abruptly change that picture.
In summary , Apple should have been outright honest and crystal clear with investors even before that letter. Being enthusiastic and excited during the November call about its business in general and China in particular has now seriously backfired for Apple.
In reality, the market it is operating in has substantially changed and distances itself from the rosy descriptions of Tim Cook earlier in 2018. Apple's pricing experiments have apparently reached its limits, at least as long as no new enticing features accompany new iPhone releases.
The iPhone itself is certainly not dead and overall Apple is still generating loads of sales and profits, but for a business the size of Apple to see its dominant product drop 15% Y/Y in its strongest quarter is certainly an alarming sign .
The company needs to listen to this wake-up call and release real innovations for its next iPhone while also ensuring that it has something attractive to offer for the lower-end market.
If Apple really wants to transform itself into a services company, it needs to ensure that the user base continues to grow and it will certainly need the low-end smartphone market for that endeavor to work out.
I have trimmed my position in Apple following the disastrous letter to investors and will closely eye the company's Q2 guidance and its earnings call. Apple has lost its mojo for now but it can certainly get it back.
